newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais to sell Bergamasco stake.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais to sell Bergamasco stake.

text.p: Pursuing its spate of asset disposals, French state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais said on Tuesday it planned to sell its majority stake in Italy's Credito Bergamasco as part of a refocusing of its activities ahead of privatisation.
Credit Lyonnais said the northern Italian-based bank would be put up for sale in the next few days but that it would remain a presence in Italy in the corporate finance field.

Credit Lyonnais has been under heavy pressure to sell non-French assets to meet conditions set by the European Commission for approving state aid to the bank, which almost collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of its lending excesses.
Once the world's largest bank outside Japan, the bank plans to limit its retail banking activities to France and focus on wholesale banking and capital market operations internationally.
Credito Bergamasco, whose balance sheet totals 43 billion francs ($7.5 billion), has a total stock market value of around 5.7 billion francs and had a 1996 net profit of 340 million francs.
Although considered a healthy operation, the sale of Credit Lyonnais' 56.8 percent stake in Credito Bergamasco is expected to trigger a capital loss, banking analysts said.
The bank was acquired in 1989 during Credit Lyonnais' asset buying spree which took place when prices were at their peak.

The planned sale follows the bank's announcement last month it was putting its 53.4 percent stake in Irish specialist finance group Woodchester Investments Plc on the block. In February, it said it was selling Credit Lyonnais Bank Sverige AB to Sweden's Trygg-Banken AB.

Analysts said the latest sale announcement was expected. "It's no surprise it has got to go," said one, adding who would buy the stake was anybody's guess. "It could be a domestic Italian bank wishing to expand or a foreign bank seeking to gain a foothold in the Italian market," he said.

Credit Lyonnais, meanwhile, said it had no comment on a report in the afternoon daily Le Monde that talks between the bank and the government on a long-awaited plan to privatise the bank were at an impasse. The finance ministry also would not comment.
But a source close to the discussions said: "It is true there are tensions."

The government said on Monday it was close to submitting the proposal to the European Commission for clearance but the bank issued a statement later in the day saying the plan, initially promised to Brussels for February, had not been finalised.

The newspaper said the two sides were at odds over Finance Minister Jean Arthuis' refusal earlier this month to recapitalise the bank to boost its solvency ratios and to offset capital losses from asset sales demanded by the European Union.
The government, which has bailed out the bank twice, had been expected to inject 10 billion francs more into Credit Lyonnais ahead of its sale, targeted for late 1998.
Bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade has long argued it needs to be recapitalised to attract a buyer.
The paper said chances of completing the plan had been complicated by President Jacques Chirac's announcement on Monday of a snap parliamentary election.
Le Monde said relations between Arthuis and Peyrelevade were "very difficult," adding Arthuis tried in vain during the past few months to find "an acceptable successor" to Peyrelevade.
Peyrelevade has said the bank cannot endanger its future by selling off strategic operations and has suggested he could resign if the bank's viability were threatened.
